S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
examples: Continually procrastinates or is reluctant to start writing long reports or complex homework.
Avoids activities that require long periods of concentration, such as reading books or studying.
Passes off tasks that require complex thinking or planning to others.
Gets annoyed or resists when asked to start a task that requires significant mental effort.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattentive symptoms that interfere with functioning across important settings, without the hyperactive-impulsive symptoms being the main clinical picture. It commonly becomes more apparent when external structure decreases or responsibilities increase, and it is distinguished from ordinary distractibility by its chronicity, pervasiveness, and functional impairment rather than by a single lapse or temporary stress reaction.

patient.stressor: After the death of a close friend who had co-led senior art walks with him, Jason took over the museum liaison duties alone and tried to preserve their shared routines with printed maps, checklists, and carefully labeled folders. Over the next two years and four months, the added solo coordination exposed long-standing inattentive tendencies: he lost workshop materials and camera accessories, drifted during planning conversations, left volunteer tasks partly completed, and put off reading-heavy preparation for gallery talks. Because the impairment remained mostly limited to volunteering and home projects but was persistent enough to worry him, Jason brought it up with his primary care doctor, who referred him to psychiatry for assessment.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
S003.manifestation: What brings me in is that people at the museum will be talking right to me about the next art walk, and I’ll be looking at them, but then I realize I missed the middle of what they said and have to ask them to run it by me again.

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: I can sit down with a gallery packet or a set of notes and start out fine, but after a few minutes my eyes keep moving over the page while my mind has wandered off and I have to read the same part again.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: When someone gives me a few things to handle for the volunteer group, I’ll do the first part, like printing the maps, but then I may forget to call the museum desk or leave the folders half-ready until someone reminds me.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
S006.manifestation: If I know I need to read through a long exhibit description or plan out a talk, I keep finding little chores around the house to do first because sitting with all that reading feels like pulling teeth.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: I’m always putting down the camera battery, name tags, or the envelope with sign-up sheets somewhere safe and then spending half the morning retracing my steps to find them.

add_requirements.Onset prior to age 12 years: Even back in grade school, my report cards said things like “daydreams” and “needs reminders to finish work,” and my mother used to sit beside me to keep me on track with homework before I was twelve.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: The museum group has had to quietly shift some planning pieces away from me, and I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to.
add_requirements.duration: It’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months, since my friend died and I took over the museum liaison duties by myself.
